standard_prerequisites.name: The characterization of the normalization as the universal object for factorizations through a locally birational integral morphism, cited from the same chapter
standard_prerequisites.use: Applies to the composite of the second normalization with the first to produce a canonical morphism between them.

standard_prerequisites.name: The uniqueness part of the same characterization, which is what makes the two morphisms mutually inverse
standard_prerequisites.use: Identifies the canonical morphism and its companion as inverse to one another.

core_obligations: Apply the universal property: if the second normalization is a morphism from the source onto an intermediate scheme over the first normalization, then applying the characterization to the composite with the first normalization produces a canonical morphism from the first normalization to the second (proof lines 14057-14061).

Conclude: the canonical morphism and the structure morphism of the second normalization are mutually inverse, by uniqueness of the factorization in the characterization, so the two schemes are the same up to canonical isomorphism (proof lines 14062-14064).
proof_roadmap: Produce a canonical morphism between the two normalizations by the universal property and conclude with the uniqueness of the factorization (proof lines 14057-14064).
difficulty_reason: The lemma says that normalizing a base in a quasi-compact quasi-separated morphism and then normalizing the result in the same source returns the same scheme (statement lines 14050-14055). The counted proof is short and complete: the universal property of the normalization applied to the composite of the second normalization with the first gives a canonical morphism in the reverse direction, and uniqueness of the factorization shows that it is inverse to the structure morphism of the second normalization (proof lines 14057-14064). It is H2: the two steps are carried out in the counted span, with the cited input being the characterization of the normalization by its universal property.
